query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified, equiatomic, Co‐free FeNiCrMn, dynamic mechanical behavior is controlled by a strain‐rate and temperature–dependent clustering-to-ordering transition within shear bands that modulates dislocation mobility, thereby preserving a favorable strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized, solidified equiatomic FeNiCrMn with a primarily disordered matrix (e.g., BCC or FCC, as produced by standard casting and homogenization) with minimal pre‐existing chemical short-range order.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to uniaxial deformation under both compressive and tensile loading at varying strain rates (ranging from quasi-static to high dynamic rates) and temperatures (from cryogenic ~77 K to elevated temperatures up to ~700–1000 K).
generation.conditions: Tests performed under controlled temperature environments and constant strain rates with identical processing histories to ensure comparable initial defect distributions; parallel tensile tests serve as controls.
generation.structural_mediator: Shear band regions where strain localization leads to atomic-scale clustering that can transition from a disordered to a more chemically ordered arrangement under compressive loading.
generation.mechanism: Under high strain-rate compressive loading, localized shear banding produces intense plastic deformation that initially induces a disordered clustering of atoms. As deformation continues, favorable atomic rearrangements enable a clustering-to-ordering transition within these bands. This transition reduces the local lattice distortion, retards dislocation motion in a way that increases strain hardening, and preserves ductility despite enhanced strength. In contrast, tensile loading lacks the same degree of shear localization and thus does not foster this transition.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under compressive loading, especially at higher strain rates and lower temperatures, specimens will exhibit higher peak flow stresses and an increased strain hardening rate associated with the transition from disordered clusters to ordered atomic arrangements. Tensile loading will not show this transition, resulting in a lower stress response. Thus, a distinct dynamic signature (i.e., clustering-to-ordering transition observed via microstructural probes coupled with mechanical response differences) will be evident only under conditions where shear banding is pronounced.
generation.baseline: Deformation behavior under quasi-static loading at room temperature where minimal shear localization occurs and the alloy retains its predominantly disordered state, resulting in lower peak stresses and less pronounced strain hardening.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be observable only in samples with minimal extrinsic defects or secondary phase precipitates; significant variations in processing history, contamination, or phase separation may obscure the clustering-to-ordering transition and alter the dynamic response.
generation.uncertainty: The precise strain-rate and temperature thresholds at which the clustering-to-ordering transition occurs in FeNiCrMn are not well defined, and it is uncertain whether the phenomena observed in Co-containing HEAs (such as Al0.1CrCoFeNi) fully translate to the Co-free system.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of solidified FeNiCrMn specimens with identical, well-characterized microstructures. Perform uniaxial compression tests at multiple strain rates (from ~10⁻³ s⁻¹ up to high dynamic rates) and temperatures (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 700 K). Employ in-situ techniques such as transmission electron microscopy or synchrotron X-ray scattering during deformation to monitor atomic-scale clustering and ordering in shear bands. Conduct parallel tensile tests under the same conditions as controls.
measurements: Flow stress curves and strain hardening rates
In-situ microstructural measurements (TEM or X-ray scattering) focusing on regions of shear localization
Post-deformation analysis using atom probe tomography or high-resolution electron microscopy to quantify the extent of chemical ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under compressive loading, no significant differences in atomic-scale clustering and ordering are detected across the range of strain rates and temperatures compared to the quasi-static baseline, or if similar clustering transitions are observed in tensile loading (where shear banding is minimal), then the proposed mechanism—i.e., that a strain rate and temperature–dependent clustering-to-ordering transition underlies the dynamic behavior—would be falsified.
